turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nora, Aoife, in you come out of that rain. Grand soft day if you like drowning.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm wringing wet, doctor. The brolly turned inside out at the roundabout. Are you well yourself?
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not a bother. Have a seat there. What's brought the two of you in?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the legs. They're swelled up like puddings, the two of them, and I get puffed.
[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She has to stop halfway up the stairs at home. I filled the pill box this morning and I still don't trust it, so I came with her.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Before all that, did you see little Cian on the hurling on Sunday? My grandson, eight years of age, and he's already shouting at the referee.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): I had it on in the background for a bit.

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Two points he got, and one of them from out on the wing with his left, and he's right-handed. His father went hoarse. They had tea and ham sandwiches in the clubhouse after, and the rain was hopping off the roof.
[SEG0009] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Mam, leave the match.

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm nearly done. The referee was Tommy Hegarty's young lad from our own parish. Tommy used to cut our grass when his back was right. The jersey was down to Cian's knees and his boots were caked in muck, and they still made him man of the match, if you wouldn't mind.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): And the weather, doctor, it's been pure miserable. I had the good coat on me and it's destroyed. Mrs Dunne next door says her dog won't even go out in it.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sounds like a great day out for him all the same. We'll park the hurling there. Tell me about these legs.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): The two ankles, and it creeps up towards the shins by evening. I'd say two weeks. Ah no, I'm a liar, it's a good month now.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): A month. Both sides, worse by evening. Does anything ease it?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): If I put the feet up on the stool after the news, they go down a small bit. In the morning they're not as bad.
[SEG0016] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The shoes don't go on by teatime. She's in the slippers all evening.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the puffing, is that new with the swelling?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): On the stairs mostly. I have to stop and hold the rail. On the flat I'm grand enough.
[SEG0019] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She used to take the stairs in one go. Not for the last month.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): How are you sleeping? How many pillows?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Two pillows now. I was always a one-pillow woman. If I slip down I feel a bit stuffed.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any pain in the chest with that?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No pain in the chest. Not a twinge.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Cough? Phlegm? Wheeze?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough. I'm clear that way.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): And when you stand up, any dizziness?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh now, if I hop up off the chair I go woozy for a second. That's the last while, maybe a fortnight. Then it passes, like.
[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I've seen her grab the table. She hasn't fallen, thank God.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever, or pain when you pass water?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever, and the waterworks are grand. I go a bit more because of the water tablet, that's all.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. You have the heart failure a few years, and the blood pressure. Still the case?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): That's it. The heart failure, and the pressure. I'm under Dr Brennan for the heart, but I haven't seen him since the winter.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any operations along the way?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): The gallbladder, years ago, keyhole. Nothing since. My father went with a heart attack at seventy, but sure that was his own doing, he lived on rashers.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll note that. Do you smoke, or take a drink?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): I never smoked in my life. Drink, hardly at all, a small sherry at Christmas if there's trifle.
[SEG0037] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She lives with me. I do the dinners and the tablets. She's not on her own.

[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. Let's go through the tablets, because the letter in front of me and what people actually swallow are often two different stories. The letter says furosemide twenty milligrams, one every morning. The water tablet.
[SEG0039] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That's not what we've got, doctor. The box from the chemist says forty milligrams, and I put one in the morning slot. I don't know where twenty came from.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): I just take what she sets out. I couldn't tell you the milligrams. It's the little yellow water one.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the letter has twenty and the box has forty, and we can't call it either way till I see the box. We'll come back to what I'll write. What else is in the pill box?

[SEG0042] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ramipril, for the blood pressure. Two and a half milligrams. No, sorry, I'm looking at the old strength in my head, they put her up, it's five milligrams, one in the morning.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Five milligrams once in the morning. Anything else of the ramipril?

[SEG0044] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): This is the bit I'm mortified about. There was an old bottle of the two and a half still in the press, and I thought it was a separate tablet, so I was putting one of those in at night as well. Only for a few days. I binned it this morning when I read the label properly.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): I didn't know I was getting two. I thought the night one was for sleeping or something. Sure I can't read the tiny writing.

[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): So you may have had an extra ramipril at night for a few days, and we're not certain how many nights. We'll treat the proper dose as five milligrams once each morning. Is there another tablet you can't name?
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): There's a little white one, tiny yoke, after the breakfast. Every day. I haven't a clue what it is.

[SEG0048] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The label is washed out. I can't read a word of it. I just keep putting the little white one in the box because it was in the cupboard with the others, and I've no idea what it's for.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then I won't guess. Bring me that box next time and we'll identify it. Anything that was stopped?
[SEG0050] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The cholesterol one. I nearly said simvastatin there. No, it was atorvastatin. Dr Brennan in the hospital stopped it because her legs were aching.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): The aches went off after he stopped it, thank God. When was that, Aoife? After Christmas? I couldn't put a date on it.
[SEG0052] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I think February, but I haven't the discharge letter, so I wouldn't swear to the month.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stopped, and the date is unclear. Any allergies I should know before I prescribe?
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Not a one. I can take whatever you throw at me. No allergies.
[SEG0055] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Mam, the penicillin. You came out in a rash all over in the hospital years ago, and they told you never to take penicillin again.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): That was the heat, Aoife, the ward was roasting. I'm not allergic to penicillin. I don't care what they wrote.
[SEG0057] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm only saying what they told us. I wasn't going to let it go unsaid.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll record it as disputed, not as a definite allergy, and I won't be using penicillin today anyway. Let me have a look at you. Shoes off, thanks.
[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): There's pitting oedema on both sides, up to about the middle of the shin. Your lungs are clear, no crackles. Heart sounds are regular, no murmur.
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pulse is ninety. Hang on, let me count that again. No, it's eighty-eight. And the blood pressure today is one thirty-six over seventy-eight.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that bad? My neighbour says once you're over a hundred you're in trouble, but she says a lot of things. She told me to eat beetroot.
[SEG0062] person_1 (DOCTOR): One thirty-six over seventy-eight is acceptable for you today. Forget the beetroot for a minute. Let me say back what I've heard, and correct me.

[SEG0063] person_1 (DOCTOR): Swelling of both legs for a month, worse by evening and a bit better with the feet up, breathless on the stairs the same length of time, two pillows, no chest pain and no cough. Woozy on standing for about a fortnight. Heart failure and the blood pressure are ongoing, gallbladder out years ago. You live with Aoife and you never smoked.
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the lot. And Cian got man of the match, but you said park that.

[SEG0065] person_1 (DOCTOR): The water tablet is furosemide, the letter says twenty milligrams and the box says forty, so that dose is not agreed. Ramipril five milligrams in the morning, plus an extra night-time one for a few days that's now binned, and a little white tablet after breakfast that nobody can name. Atorvastatin was stopped by Dr Brennan, date unclear, aches gone. The penicillin rash is disputed between the two of you.
[SEG0066] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That's fair. What are you going to do?

[SEG0067] person_1 (DOCTOR): My impression is provisional, that fluid is building up again from the heart failure, and the dizziness might be the tablets or just standing up too fast, I can't separate those yet. First thought, with the extra ramipril and the dizziness, I was going to stop the ramipril altogether.

[SEG0068] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The dizziness was there before I added the night one. It was only four days, and the old bottle is in the bin since this morning. She needs the blood pressure tablet, Dr Brennan was very firm about it.
[SEG0069] person_1 (DOCTOR): All right. I won't stop the ramipril. Stay on five milligrams once every morning, and nothing of it at night.
[SEG0070] person_1 (DOCTOR): For the fluid, I was going to put the furosemide up to eighty milligrams.
[SEG0071] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): They tried a bigger dose before and she went very wobbly, and Dr Brennan said the kidneys were a bit touchy. I'd be afraid of eighty.
[SEG0072] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't want to be falling around the kitchen, doctor.

[SEG0073] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then scratch the eighty, that's me changing the plan. I'll write furosemide forty milligrams, one each morning, so there's one clear dose from here, and I won't push it higher until I see the kidneys.
[SEG0074] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll also send you for a blood test, kidney function and potassium, this week. I nearly said a chest x-ray, but the lungs are clear so we won't do that.
[SEG0075] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I can bring her down to the blood place Thursday.
[SEG0076] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thursday is fine. Bring the little white tablet in its box when you come back, and throw nothing else out before I see it.
[SEG0077] person_2 (PATIENT): And if I get worse?

[SEG0078] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the breathing gets much worse, or you get chest pain, or you faint, don't wait for me, go to the emergency department. Keep the feet up in the evenings as you've been doing. Come back here in two weeks and we'll look at the bloods and that white tablet.
[SEG0079] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Grand. Aoife will have me organised. Tell Cian I was talking about his points, he'll be delighted.
[SEG0080] person_1 (DOCTOR): I will. Mind yourselves on the way out, the path is slippy.

clinical_actions.description: Prescribe furosemide 40 mg once each morning after deciding against an increase to 80 mg, and do not push the dose higher until the kidney results are seen
Blood test for kidney function and potassium
Considered stopping ramipril altogether because of the extra dose and dizziness, then decided not to stop it; stay on 5 mg once every morning and take none at night
Go to the emergency department if breathing gets much worse, chest pain occurs, or she faints
Keep the feet up in the evenings
Bring the little white tablet in its box and do not throw other medicines out before review
Chest x-ray considered but not ordered because the lungs are clear
Follow-up consultation to review the blood results and the little white tablet

clinical_uncertainties.description: The clinic letter says furosemide 20 mg each morning but the daughter says the chemist box is 40 mg and she gives one each morning.
An extra night-time ramipril 2.5 mg from an old bottle was added for a few days, later stated as four days, and it is not certain how many of those doses were taken; the bottle was binned.
Neither the patient nor her daughter can name the little white tablet taken after breakfast because the label cannot be read.
No one can date when atorvastatin was stopped; the patient suggested after Christmas but could not give a date, and the daughter thinks February but will not swear to the month.
The patient denies any allergy while her daughter recalls a penicillin rash and advice never to take penicillin again.

contradictions_detected: Furosemide dose differs between the clinic letter (20 mg) and the daughter (40 mg).
Patient denies allergies while the daughter reports a penicillin rash.

spec.situation: Older patient with a live-in carer or daughter who manages the pill box; names of tablets are described ('the little white one', 'the water tablet'), one was stopped by another doctor, one is double-counted. Doctor reviews and changes one medicine.
features: tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.

bad.reason: Patient did not explicitly deny phlegm.
Patient did not explicitly deny wheeze.

omissions.text: Breathlessness detail missing: patient is 'grand enough' on the flat; shortness of breath is mainly on stairs.
Orthostatic dizziness detail missing: when she stands up quickly from a chair she feels woozy for a second, and it then passes.
Increased urination due to the water tablet was stated ('I go a bit more because of the water tablet').
Family history is incomplete/wrongly recorded: father died of a heart attack at age 70.
Ramipril dosing error specifics missing: the extra night-time tablet was ramipril 2.5 mg from an old bottle, taken for only a few days.
Atorvastatin stop timing was estimated as around February / after Christmas, though uncertain.
Examination detail missing: lungs were clear, not just 'no crackles'.
The doctor considered but then changed plans: initially thought of stopping ramipril altogether because of dizziness and extra ramipril use, but decided not to after discussion.

The doctor considered increasing furosemide to 80 mg but changed the plan after family/patient concern about prior wobbliness and kidney sensitivity; decided not to increase beyond 40 mg until kidney results are available.
A real concern/disagreement was expressed that higher-dose furosemide had previously made her very wobbly and Dr Brennan had said her kidneys were 'a bit touchy'.
Investigation change of plan missing: the doctor nearly ordered a chest x-ray but decided against it because the lungs were clear.
Follow-up purpose missing: return in two weeks specifically to review the blood results and identify/review the little white tablet.
